source: OECD (2025), Health at a Glance 2025: OECD Indicators, OECD Publishing, Paris
framing: Gap framing: every figure is what is NOT covered, NOT satisfied or unmet. Gap figures are 100 minus the published figure.
rule: HAL may phrase these facts freely but must not state any figure, ranking or claim that is not in this list. Verbatim report sentences may name other countries; only what they say about this country may be used.

facts.text: 39% of people in Finland were NOT satisfied with the availability of quality healthcare where they live in 2024, versus an OECD average of 36%; satisfaction has deteriorated over the past decade.
19% of health spending in Finland was NOT covered by government or compulsory insurance schemes in 2023, versus an OECD average of 24.9%.
8.5% of people in Finland reported unmet medical care needs due to cost, distance or waiting times in 2024 (average of 28 OECD countries: 3.4%).
4% of hospital care costs in Finland were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 11% on average in the OECD.
13% of outpatient medical care costs in Finland were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 22% on average in the OECD.
57% of dental care costs in Finland were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 68% on average in the OECD.
42% of pharmaceutical costs in Finland were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 42% on average in the OECD.

However, over 8% of the population reported unmet care needs in Latvia (8.4%), Estonia (8.5%), Finland (8.6%), Canada (9.1%) and Greece (12.1%), while in Germany, the Netherlands and Czechia, fewer than 1% of the population reported unmet needs for medical care.
In Latvia, Estonia and Finland, more than 5% of the population cited waiting times as a barrier.
The income gradient was largest in Greece, Latvia and Finland, with a difference of over 8 percentage points in the population reporting unmet needs between the lowest and highest income quintiles.

In Greece, more than one in six people in the lowest income quintile reported unmet medical care needs, and in Estonia, Finland and Latvia this proportion reaches more than one in ten people in the lowest income quintile.
This is especially notable in Finland, Lithuania, Ireland, Greece, Spain and France, where unmet medical care needs due to waiting times increased by 1.4 percentage points or more since 2019.

In Canada, Finland, Sweden, the United Kingdom and the United States, the relatively low number of consultations can be explained in part by the enhanced role that nurses and other health professionals play in primary care – notably in management of patients with chronic diseases and in dealing with patients with minor health issues.
Such countries tend to have higher consultation rates than those countries where doctors are mainly paid by salaries or capitation (such as Denmark, Finland, Mexico and Sweden).

The average rate of antihypertensive prescribing increased by 4 percentage points from 2013 to 2023 across OECD countries with available data, reflecting improved adherence to clinical guidelines, with the improvement particularly notable in Finland.

In 2023, PHC represented 14% of all health spending on average across OECD countries, ranging from 10% or less in Switzerland, the Netherlands, Luxembourg and the Slovak Republic to around 20% in Lithuania, Estonia and Finland (Figure 7.16).

This covers a wide range of facilities with most spending related to either medical practices including GPs and specialists (as in Austria, France and Germany) or ambulatory healthcare centres (as in Finland, Ireland and Sweden).

Overall, every third health dollar was spent on ambulatory providers in Belgium, Mexico, Finland, Luxembourg and the United States but this share was below 20% in Türkiye, Greece and the Slovak Republic.
The latter provider group plays a much more central role in the health systems in the Netherlands, Sweden and Finland than elsewhere.
In Finland and Denmark, outpatient care accounts for more than half of hospital expenditure, since specialists typically receive patients in hospital outpatient departments.
